JSON: Name: curvnet_pipeline Title: CurvNet: latent contour representation with iterative synthetic-data engine for automatic Cobb angle estimation from spinal X-rays Short Hypothesis: A low-rank latent contour representation of spinal segment landmarks combined with anchor-box classification and iterative augmentation using privacy-screened diffusion-generated images reduces Cobb angle estimation symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE) by at least 10% relative to representative regression-, segmentation-, and landmark-based baselines on standard spine X-ray benchmarks. Related Work: Existing automatic Cobb-angle methods fall into three dominant paradigms: regression-based approaches that regress angles or bounding boxes directly from image features, segmentation-based approaches that produce pixel-level spinal masks which are post-processed to derive angles, and landmark-based approaches that detect vertebral corners/landmarks and compute angles geometrically. Regression approaches are compact but rely on rectangular or block-shaped assumptions that fail for wedge-shaped or irregular vertebrae. Segmentation methods preserve spatial detail but are sensitive to image noise, contrast variation and often produce connected/fragmented masks that corrupt downstream angle estimation. Landmark detectors yield precise geometric measures when well trained but require extensive high-quality annotations and degrade on small datasets. For training-data scarcity and domain coverage, generative approaches (GANs, diffusion models) have been proposed; GANs can suffer from mode collapse and limited coverage, while diffusion models improve realism but risk memorization of training examples. Semi-supervised pseudo-labeling and multi-stage annotation pipelines address annotation cost but are vulnerable to noisy pseudo-labels and require careful selection criteria. Abstract: This pipeline integrates a latent low-rank contour representation with a contour-detection network and an iterative synthetic-data engine to improve automatic Cobb angle estimation from AP spinal X-rays. The contour representation parameterizes each spinal segment as a fixed-vertex contour projected into a compact eigen-spine basis learned by singular value decomposition; a network jointly regresses latent contour coefficients and classifies positive anchor boxes to recover segment contours. The iterative data engine augments training with text- and latent-diffusion-generated X-rays, applies automated filtering and manual-assisted correction, and enforces a privacy-aware similarity review to exclude high-similarity generated images. The combined approach targets three failure modes of prior work—rectangular box approximation, segmentation mask fragmentation, and limited annotated data—by improving contour fidelity and increasing training diversity without exposing real patient images. Expected outcomes are reduced Cobb angle estimation error and improved robustness across curve types, with an empirically measurable privacy-risk profile for the generated dataset. Experiments: Datasets: AASCE2019 (481 train / 128 test) for public benchmarking; Spinal2023 (700 train / 204 test) as private clinical data for model pretraining; Spinal-AI2024 (16,000 train / 4,000 test) generated dataset used for augmentation and ablation. Baselines: representative methods from three paradigms: (1) regression baseline: Faster-RCNN style box regression that predicts rectangular spine blocks and direct maximum-angle regression; (2) segmentation baseline: U-Net instance segmentation producing spinal masks followed by angle extraction; (3) landmark baseline: heatmap-based landmark detector (hourglass/HRNet style) predicting 68 landmarks; (4) generative baseline for data augmentation: StyleGAN2-ADA generated images used in place of diffusion-generated images. Evaluation metrics: symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE) for maximum and regional (PT, MT, TL/L) Cobb angles; Euclidean distance (ED) for landmark placement; object detection metrics AP and AR for segment detection; Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) for generated image realism; SSIM and pixel-similarity (PS) and combined comprehensive similarity (CS) for privacy assessment. Training setup: train all detectors using SGD with momentum 0.9 and weight decay 5e-4; initial LR 1e-3 with polynomial decay; 100 epochs pretrain on Spinal2023 then fine-tune with augmented datasets; diffusion model: fine-tune latent diffusion U-Net for 50 epochs with AdamW lr=2e-5, classifier-free guidance scale=7.5; input image resolution 512x512 for detectors; batch sizes chosen to saturate a 24GB GPU (typical batch 8). Primary comparisons: (A) CurvNet trained only on Spinal2023 versus each baseline trained only on Spinal2023; (B) CurvNet trained on Spinal2023 augmented with Spinal-AI2024 versus each baseline similarly augmented. Ablation studies: (1) latent basis dimension M ∈ {4,8,16,32}; (2) classification branch ablated vs included; (3) regression dense vs sparse assignment vs both; (4) iterative data-engine iterations 0..6 to measure convergence; (5) effect of diffusion-generated images vs StyleGAN2-ADA images; (6) privacy threshold τ_CS ∈ {0.5,0.6,0.7} for dataset inclusion and its effect on SMAPE and CS. Statistical analysis: report mean±std over 5 runs with different random seeds and perform paired t-tests comparing CurvNet to best baseline (α=0.05). Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Privacy leakage: diffusion-generated images may memorize and reproduce training examples, causing re-identification risk if similarity thresholds are insufficient. 2) Annotation noise: pseudo-labeling and automatic selection can propagate incorrect contours leading to biased training. 3) Cervical mislocalization: inclusion of cervical vertebrae in PT region causes large PT-angle overestimation. 4) Domain shift: model trained on AP X-rays with specific acquisition settings may not generalize to lateral views or different hospital protocols. 5) Rare-case scarcity: low-frequency extreme Cobb angles (>45° or atypical curve morphologies) may be underrepresented in generated and real training data, limiting performance on severe cases. 6) Low-rank approximation limits: truncation of eigen-spines can lose fine local contour detail required for precise landmark placement. 7) Compute and scalability: training diffusion generators and large detectors requires substantial GPU resources and time. 8) Evaluation bias: using generated data in both training and test selection risks overestimating generalization if generated-test images are not strictly separated or sufficiently diverse. 9) Regulatory and ethical constraints: deployment in clinical workflows faces legal, validation, and interpretability requirements not addressed by the pipeline.
